utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Loncar. Are you receiving the sound from our interpretation? TECHNICIAN: [In Belgrade] There's no translation as of yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say, we can hear translation on B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can. Good morning, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination will now continue. You were being asked questions by Mr. Cepic yesterday and he will continue now. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I may have a moment. Yesterday we were discussing Podujevo and the crisis which erupted when the -- when one of the Serbs was killed in that area. Mr. Ciaglinski mentioned that there were 1 to 2.000 KLA fighters there, equipped and with ammunition. In paragraph 49 of your statement you stated that several days later the Army of Yugoslavia arrived with no intention to use tanks. Mr. Drewienkiewicz accused the Serb side for excessive use of force subsequently. The term of "the excessive use of force," could you please explain it to us and can you give us your assessment of Mr. Drewienkiewicz's opinion for the army having used excessive force.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to correct something. The army was not deployed with tanks. It was an exercise which had been planned and announced to the OSCE, and it had to do with the training of the new generation of tank operators, and they were exercising in the vicinity of Podujevo. They thought it as a tout of force, as an excessive use of force, but it was merely by chance that both the army and the police were there at the same time, although their tasks differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 62 of your statement, you state that the Kosovo Verification Mission also assessed that as the excessive use of force by Serb forces under the circumstances in which the KLA actually attacked the Serb forces. You also stated that you know of no facts which could corroborate that. Could you please explain this term "excessive use of force," and did it occur indeed, either carried out by the police or the army in the relevant time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When discussing any incident, when discussions were held between me and my team and the OSCE, they never said that proportionate force was used; they always kept saying that it was excessive. And I was under the impression that we, according to them, should have sent two soldiers or two policemen, and even then they would call it excessive use of force. Therefore, their assessment was based on their opinion that we needed to use less forces, less troops; however, my opinion was to use what was available, and I believe that even those troops were insufficient to try and confront the situation that was on their hands at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Another thing that I wanted to clarify as regards this. Mr. Drewienkiewicz in his statement states that you suggested that APCs be used, two APCs and 13 Pinzgauers, to deal with the situation in Podujevo. Further on he states that there were negotiations at Walker's office, and while you were negotiating there was an incursion into the village and, once having received that information, Walker started shouting at you and kicked you out of his office. Can you tell us precisely what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he didn't kick me out and I wouldn't have allowed me to. I wouldn't have been kicked out by anyone. Mr. Walker was a diplomat and he conversed at that level. We had an argument a discussion. I was convinced that he was given wrong information [Realtime transcript read in error, "I was given wrong information"] on the engagement of our mechanised forces, as regards the 11 APCs and so on. I left the meeting because I was pressured by the information, misinformation he received. And since he wouldn't listen to my explanations, I left. Later on we discussed it further and clarified things because what was forwarded to the meeting at that very moment was incorrect, it was forwarded by means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a significant transcript mistake at 3, 17, where it says, "I was given the wrong information." He said, "I have the impression -- I had the impression he was given the wrong information."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was under the impression that Mr. Walker had been given wrong information during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Another thing to clarify concerning Podujevo. Both Mr. Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Ciaglinski mentioned the so-called Tenkovsko Brdo, tank hill, and that you discussed that topic with them. Do you remember this so-called tank hill? It was actually a terrorist location where there were numerous trenches, and there were daily terrorist attacks from there against the police, the army, and citizens.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are down on the road facing the tank hill, you could see with the naked eye, and, especially with the binoculars, you could confirm what Mr. Ciaglinski and Drewienkiewicz said. It was a dominating feature in that area and there were strong fortifications and some terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To be clear, General, they didn't state it was a terrorist stronghold. It was me who stated it; however, they said that such a tank hill did in fact exist, but at the later stage the Army of Yugoslavia was deployed there. I wanted to know about the period before the 22nd of December, whether it was a terrorist stronghold?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. When I travelled between Pristina and Belgrade, I could see for myself there. They moved about freely, and their forces were up at the tank hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, you've mentioned that there was an exercise in place by the Army of Yugoslavia, a tank exercise between Pristina, Podujevo, and Prepolac; and on the 22nd of December on that axis, or rather, at the tank hill, a tank was damaged. It was put out of operation, and a smaller group of 20 soldiers remained at the tank to guard it until conditions improved, so as to be able to repair it. And that is why the tank hill was termed in that way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Loncar. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an objection to the form of the question. Mr. Cepic seems to be testifying. If he would cite a reference to what he's saying I wouldn't have a problem but as it stands it sounds like it's just his evidence about what happened on December 22nd. If he puts it in the form of the question, I don't have an objection about that either, but not the way he's doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is this, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question, it was page 5, line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but which paragraph is it in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, this concerns Mr. Ciaglinski's and Mr. Drewienkiewicz's statements. Mr. Drewienkiewicz in paragraph 104 mentions the tank hill. Mr. Ciaglinski mentions it on several occasions, including during his cross-examination; he mentioned the term tank hill. This was the basis for my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but what is the question you're about to ask because it just sounds as if you're giving evidence; it doesn't sound as if it's coming to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can reformulate, with your leave, paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay. Try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you know why that feature is or was called tank hill?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the tank which had been left behind and because of that event. That exercise, the tank exercise, had been announced to the OSCE and they dispatched their monitors to follow the situation. The tank was damaged during the exercise, and later on was pulled out from the location of tank hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you know that on that occasion three VJ soldiers were injured when the tank was damaged?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Drewienkiewicz in his statement mentions that he demanded a meeting be held with the generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, just one correction for transcript. The witness answered: "Yes, I know," not, "Yes, I did." Page number 6, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it comes to the same thing, Mr. Cepic, so there's no harm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To go back to my previous question, General, did Mr. Drewienkiewicz ask for a meeting to be called with Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic? You said that due to their recent promotion, no meeting could be held or discussed. It was out of the question. Were you ever forwarded such a request by Drewienkiewicz?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the case we have been discussing, I cannot be fully certain as to whether he demanded such a meeting or not. It was only on one other occasion that Drewienkiewicz asked to see either Pavkovic or Lazarevic. As for this particular instance, I don't think he asked to see them but I cannot be certain. Had he asked to see them, believe me, I would have made it possible for him. If not, to have Lazarevic or Pavkovic there, then at least someone else from the top of the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, is it correct to say that one of the basic tasks of the KVM was to verify the cease-fire and any conflict in the field?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was their basic and primary goal -- task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As regards the touring of facilities and the restricted area of movement in the border belt, did you know that for separate visits and inspection of the facilities and barracks, such activities had to be notified and given permission by the Pristina Corps was it was not part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that such a procedure was in place that the KVM representatives can tour units with a mandatory presence of an officer from that unit or corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that touring of the units in the border area had to be announced previously and that such monitors must have been escorted by an officer because of the possibility of ambush or an encounter with patrols?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I particularly tried to stress those conditions and those prerequisites to both Ciaglinski and Drewienkiewicz for their own safety and for the reasons of the safety of the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The OTP put forth an exhibit number P506 describing your meeting with Mr. Drewienkiewicz on the 20th of December, 1998. The topic discussed was --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask the registrar, the court officer next to the general to show that exhibit to the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You in fact asked for a meeting with representatives of the Kosovo Verification Mission due to increasing problems created by terrorist attacks on this road, Podujevo-Pristina, so it was one of the primary topics, General, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz demanded that the Kosovo Verification Mission be notified about training exercises of the army and that the army should report it, and before that it was asked on our part that the situation in Podujevo be verified and to increase patrols on that axis. On that occasion, General Drewienkiewicz assessed the presence of the army in that area as logistically justified. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was great insecurity among the population about using those roads, and there were cases when even members of the OSCE mission were in jeopardy when using those roads. So they finally accepted this as necessary, indispensable, and even welcomed the increased control on roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 43 of your statement you stated that you were not aware of any offensive operations of the army outside of the border belt and also that the army and the MUP only responded in self-defence and carried out a small number of anti-terrorist operations, of which the OSCE was notified in advance. My question is this: Did units of the Pristina Corps fully comply with the rules of engagement and all the other regulations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Drewienkiewicz in his statement, paragraph 197, states that to the extent of his knowledge, not a single member of the OSCE mission was never allowed to enter the staff of the army or the Main Staff of the police. Mr. Loncar, in your -- paragraph 44 of your statement, you stated that Colonel Kotur had meetings even in the Main Staff of the corps with the gentlemen Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski. My question is: Were members of the mission able to visit the said buildings if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I would like to emphasise that this is incorrect. Every morning the representatives of the OSCE came to the command of the police to see Mr. Mijatovic, where Mijatovic would report to him about the incidents and situation of that day. They met with Colonel Kotur as well. It was on the premises of the police command and in my offices. It did not happen in the command of the Pristina Corps, but the demand to visit the command of the Pristina Corps was submitted. Verifiers did go, and I know that Drewienkiewicz had visited the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me if you remember the name of the mission representative who went to the building of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and met with Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my notes here, but this is verifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would it jog your memory if I mentioned the name of Guy Sands?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's Guy. I couldn't remember that name on the 28th and I didn't run into that name in my notes. But now that you told me the name of the gentleman, I remember it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 60, you stated that efforts had increased primarily on the part of the mission -- sorry, commission in concert with the KVM to gather information, among other things, about what the prevailing opinion is among civilians and what their living conditions were. Do you know that members of the KVM, together with army officers, toured Albanian villages 42 times primarily in the border belt, and talked to inhabitants of Junik, Vrmnica, Goden, Svrhe, and other villages?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was 42 times and what villages they visited, I don't know, but I know that such an activity took place. I cannot confirm the figures you mentioned, but I know it was a long-term activity that was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 61 of your statement, you stated that you had informed the Federal Commission at the meeting of the 9th of January, 1999, that the cooperation was good among regional centres of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the Army of Yugoslavia. In that sense, do you know that there was a great number of meetings and other activities between the army and the mission? My figure is that there were 101 meetings between representatives of the Pristina Corps on the one hand and the KVM on the other.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the cooperation and relationship were very intensive, because it was precisely my job to transfer obligations to a lower level. General Drewienkiewicz accepted it and visited Colonel Delic at least 15 times, which seems to confirm that there were numerous meetings. Because it's better to discuss incidents at a lower level, in more specific terms, than just to discuss it at a higher level between Walker and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know that reports from regional centres of the KVM frequently differed from assessments and positions taken by the top of the mission based in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my frequent meetings that were very vociferous and very argumentative, we had reports from observers and those who were not there but wrote reports as if they had been. So there were differences between verifiers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but we have a -- some mistake in the transcript. The witness stated that Mr. Drewienkiewicz informed him about -- about the position of KVM, but his name is not in -- that should be in line -- line 20, page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, you said in your frequent meetings that were very vociferous and very argumentative, you had reports from observers and those who were not there but wrote reports as if they had been. Did you mention Drewienkiewicz in that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not saying that we had quarrels at every meeting. Everybody defended their own positions and interests quite loudly, and both Mr. Drewienkiewicz and us. But we had rather high-tempered discussions, maybe that's the best term. And Drewienkiewicz would sometimes say, "We also have verifiers that observed things from a kilometre's distance," but write about things as if they had been on the spot, and those were the differences among verifiers themselves. They report things in a way that was not authentic and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see on ELMO the Defence Exhibit 5D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: They do have a copy in Belgrade, so everything is fine. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we see a report from the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade for the 10th of March, 1999. It states that the meeting, or rather, the touring of the terrain was attended by Captain Schaffler Ferdinand and Major Aleksandar Gubarenko on behalf of the OSCE mission, and that they toured villages Bukos and Brusnik. Mr. Aleksandar Gubarenko personally could see that not a single house was burned or destroyed; whereas, they had reports saying the opposite. My question is: Do you know of events wherein KLA members trying to show the activities of Serb forces around Vucitrn and other places made fires around Vucitrn, and another example of this was the 11th of March in Podujevo. Do you know of such reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such reports came into my office and they were an integral part of the tactics of the KLA, but the verifiers became aware of those moves at a later stage and no longer went out to check out every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me to say, we have a problem in transcript again. The answer is not correct in the transcript, because with my best recollection the witness is not stated: "No longer went out to check out every time." I think that he answered something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Loncar, can you give us that answer again. You said there were such reports, came to your office. They were an integral part of the tactics of the KLA, but the verifiers got wise to that; and then what did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The verifiers realised that and later did not react to such moves by the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it comes to the same thing, Mr. Cepic. Anyway, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Succumb to pressure," I think it was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 64 of your statement you said: "Members of the so-called KLA kidnapped a large number of people." You then stated that when the so-called KLA planned an operation, they ordered civilians to leave the area, but to say that it was on account of the MUP. Do you know, General, that in the period while the mission was there, a large number of people got killed, over 180, in fact 183; members of the army, members of the police, and civilians. In fact, it was mostly civilians, 140?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. I also used aggregated statistics of the killed, kidnapped, and wounded, based on daily reports. And it's true that members of the KLA were very diligent about protecting their population. They did it in a very planned, well-thought-out way. They had good instructions and good technical moves, and it was part of that not to expose their civilians to danger. And it's true that there were members of the army and the police who were injured and wounded and targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we say that it was the KLA that instructed their own civilian population to move out or transfer somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the cooperation between the KLA and their own ethnic Albanian population; but from the military aspect, it was obvious that there was obedience and cooperation. As soon as they ordered something, it was done. So, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In paragraph 69 of your statement -- in fact, I'd like to come back to another point. You know that in those actions of the KLA of population transfers they cleansed from Serbs, disloyal Albanians, and members of ethnic and other communities, as many as 36 villages during the tenure of the mission. Do you know about that figure? ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. At meetings with top leaders of the OSCE, I often tried to prove some of my positions and allegations and claims, by presenting these reports to the verifiers, most often to General Drewienkiewicz and others, so that Walker, Drewienkiewicz, Ivanov, and Keller, and others were aware of these data.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Paragraph 69, a meeting was held in the federation palace and Sainovic's office on the 26th of February. And it was decided, amongst other things, in order to improve communications among units of the Pristina Corps of the Army of Yugoslavia and the verification mission on the other side, to assign 15 officers to units who spoke English to improve the communication. Are you aware that these new officers met with Mr. Drewienkiewicz on the 16th of March in the Pristina barracks when they met?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. I have to digress here a little bit. At that time - and it was already the end of February - it was very difficult in Kosovo and Metohija. At the time, there was public talk about bombing already, NATO attack, and all of this was present amongst all the structures of Kosovo-Metohija. And it could be sensed also in the work of the verification mission. The intensity of work had dropped off a little bit, and I was thinking and I suggested at a meeting on the 26th of February that we needed to step up and make additional efforts with the OECD, because it was our last chance so that they would not achieve their objective. So it was my proposal to the federal government to send out officers who knew English well, to improve communication; and I personally asked General Drewienkiewicz, with the agreement of Mr. Sainovic, that he should give a lecture to these officers of the VJ. And he agreed to do this, General Drewienkiewicz did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Drewienkiewicz, in his statement in paragraph 169, says that getting to know the new officers on that occasion was a time when you were quite reserved and restrained, which led him to the conclusion that there was a different attitude taken towards the commission. These measures, were they something that the federal government used in order to strengthen cooperation between the mission on one side and the Serb party or the side on the other in the way that you have just explained?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I respond I would just like to have the transcript corrected. It's line 9, page 16, it was recorded as "commission" instead of "mission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. But the witness will have the correct version, so please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This will have to be your last topic or subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know where this position comes from of Mr. Drewienkiewicz, that I was angry. I actually believed that we needed to initiate more cooperation and that we mustn't neglect that. The actual course of events was different, so I don't know why this remark of his. Although, after these measures were implemented our main objective, I repeat, was to initiate the intensity of the work of the mission, and Mr. Drewienkiewicz worked in the same way as he did before. He never showed any kind of slacking off, so there was no obstruction in the work. We all wanted -- first of all, I did. We all wanted to initiate the intensity and the quality of the work of the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you would permit me five minutes of additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we have five minutes later, you'll get it, but I cannot do that now. We've -- you've asked a lot of questions, which are not really directly questions about the personal knowledge of the witness, and I think you've had a fair opportunity to cross-examine in the context in which we agreed that this would be done at this stage. If you need to question him later, because we don't have time later today, then you will have to call him as a witness for the Defence. Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm John Ackerman, and I represent General Pavkovic. You'll remember during your testimony yesterday that you were asked a question by Judge Bonomy. The Judge asked you this: "Mr. Loncar, from a personal point of view, I entirely understand what you're saying. But I wonder if I could ask you to consider this, that rightly or wrongly, agreement had been reached between the federal authorities and the OSCE, which involved monitoring the conduct of two sides, the forces for which you were the liaison. And the OSCE had on the other side contact with the forces ranged against you, which you called terrorist. They occasionally did, but they were more commonly known as the KLA. Perhaps they saw a difficulty in trying to restrain or have any influence upon the activities of the KLA if they branded them as terrorists. Is that a possibility?" You answered: "I agree absolutely. I agree it is a possibility; however, I think it would have been fair on their part to address -- to have addressed it differently. We asked them not to insist on it; however, it was never accepted and of course, there's always a possibility such as the one you've suggested." Would you agree that if that was their purpose, to improve the influence they might have on the terrorists, on the KLA, that it was a complete failure, it didn't work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that this referred to the verification mission, to the KVM, and the OSCE based on my information and the freedom of movement in the area that was exclusively under the control of members of the KLA, first of all, Walker and Drewienkiewicz and all of those who worked on the security issues. They were welcomed there. They were -- they had freedom of action and freedom of movement. I think that they had very good relations with members of the KLA. They knew everything that was going on as far as the KLA was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the -- what I was really trying to get when I asked the question was: If what they were -- well, let me go back. You told us that you -- one of your tasks, one of your goals, was to try to get the mission to refer to the KLA as terrorists and to their acts as terrorist acts and that you didn't succeed in that, that they primarily referred to them as KLA. It was suggested that maybe that was an effort on their part, to improve their relationship with KLA so that they could exercise greater control over their activities. What I'm suggesting to you is that if that was what they were doing, it was a complete failure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what the KVM was doing in relation to the Albanian side was essential. They had to gain the confidence and trust of the members, because without their trust you couldn't work with them. They wouldn't accept anyone that they didn't trust. So what you are asking me, I believe that you are right. So my answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Ackerman, I would take the answer as no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I understand also entirely the point you're trying to make. It doesn't follow that just because they had good relations they actually had any influence, and if you want to put it as precisely as that to the witness, then you may get closer to what you're seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, General, I want to go back again to your own statement that one of your tasks there was to try to get the OSCE mission to refer to the KLA as terrorists and to their acts as terrorist acts. Now, that did not happen, and I would assume that you have -- you had a reason for that, and I wonder if you believe now that it would have made a difference, had the OSCE adopted your recommendation and referred to them as terrorists instead of KLA; and if so, what difference?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Thank you for the clarification; that is what I also believed, and this is what we wanted to achieve. If the world -- the international community and the political subjects of Europe and the United Nations are told that a state in a part of its territory is dealing with terrorists and terrorist forces, then the relations between those -- or of those subjects towards that country are quite different, political and all other kinds of relations. Not only was it a fact that in the assessment of the acts of one and the other side, that element was ruled out, that there were a lot of terrorist activities and incidents there, but this was presented as the activity of a liberation army for purposes of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one thing that you've told us in your testimony deals with the treatment the KLA was dealing upon their own people, the abductions, the kidnappings, the arrests, the killings, even, of Albanian citizens. Would you say that's characteristic of a group of freedom fighters, a liberation army, or is that more characteristic of terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't just formally accept as a task to try to present to our public and the international public that there was a terrorist force active in Kosovo, expressed through various forms of terrorist activities. But when I went to Kosovo, I understood that as being true. I accepted that as a soldier and as a human being because the way they treated non-Albanian population was something that had to be condemned. They were even more strict and rigorous towards those Albanians who supported the then-authorities of Serbia or Yugoslavia. The crimes were even harsher. And even now I would characterise that attitude as a terrorist and a criminal one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any -- do you have any view as you sit here today as to why it was the OSCE did not make greater efforts to control the KLA, the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparation for this testimony, I thought a lot about that time. But from the perspective of now, from a distance, that area and such intensely disrupted relations called for a larger number of verifiers. I think that there was supposed to be 2.000, but I believe that the maximum number that they managed to actually get from day-to-day was about 14 to 1500. So there were not enough verifiers. Second, it was a very short period of time since -- from their arrival until they finished their activities. Mr. Walker arrived at Pristina airport on the 15th of December and left already on the 23rd of March. More than two-thirds of the time of that was spent in him travelling in Europe, seeing the United Nations, going to Vienna, Brussels, and so on, because this is what he had to do. It is my conviction that a large number of verifiers were not sufficiently professional and were not up to the situation in Kosovo and Metohija at the time. I believe that I am right because as far as military matters were concerned, resolving of incidents, arbitration, most of the verifiers were civilians, and I believe that in that situation they should have been military personnel with combat experience. So all of these factors prevented the OSCE mission, and there are some other remarks also that could indicate that they did not understand very well our mentality and our problems or the Albanian mentality and problems. So all these issues were factors contributing to the mission not fulfilling its objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to a slightly different question now. I'm referring now only to the time that you were there and able to make the observations you were able to make. I want to ask you about VJ. Was the VJ involved in any offensive operations against the terrorists while you were there or were they basically in a responsive mode, responding to attacks on them by the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must state decisively that the army, the members of the Army of Yugoslavia and the Pristina Corps first of all did not conduct a single offensive action. Their activities were exclusively in response, but it's true that there were fewer attacks on the army than on the police. The army did not participate in offensive actions, just responded to incidents directed at its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 66 of your statement you said this: "Usually the most important issue for the VJ was security of the border with Albania." Can you elaborate on that at all? Explain that a little more for us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the largest number of incidents and the greatest danger to the population came from Albania. Convoys with ammunition and weapons, the freedom of movement of members of the army in either direction was something that influenced a change in the ratio of forces. So the border or the rear was completely open, was not monitored, and I can say that at the time it was under the control of the KLA and the Albanian armed forces. That is why each of our demands and each report to the OSCE members was aimed at directing their attention to deal with the problem of the border with Albania. So materiel support in weapons, equipment, evacuation of injured, KLA members, it was all done in the direction of Albania and because of the terrain, it was very difficult to monitor this area. And there were all the possibilities there available for the Albanian side to provide support to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've heard evidence in this case recently that during the OSCE mission, the VJ was increasing the number of troops in the Pristina Corps. You say in your statement that the Pristina Corps was an A formation, always a hundred percent full, and therefore no need for it to increase in number. It's possible, is it not, that the OSCE mission mistook replacements for additions to the corps? Could it be that that's the basis for their report in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strength of the Pristina Corps was specified under an agreement, and I assert that the Pristina Corps did not deviate from this agreement. Changes in the strength, I repeat, changes in the strength never happened, but there was a part of the members of the Pristina Corps that were replaced. A generation or a contingent of soldiers who were on their regular military term of duty in the Pristina Corps had expired by three months. So it wasn't 12 months but 15 months, three months extra, so these children, these soldiers needed to be replaced. An appropriate number of recruits from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came. They replaced that contingent of troops who had served their term of duty, but it was announced to the OSCE and they controlled and monitored it. In the beginning, they looked at it with a dose of skepticism. They tried to compromise us by putting the question of whether the Pristina Corps was being expanded, but I repeat it was just a question of replacing the soldiers and officers with a fresh contingent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, how many soldiers were involved in this overlap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot speak off the top of my head, but it must be noted down somewhere in the archives, in one of the reports. And it could be checked. But I am positive that the number of those who left equalled the number of those who arrived. I listened to what Mr. Drewienkiewicz said, and he was satisfied with the content, meaning -- with the numbers, meaning that the number of those replaced was unchanged compared to the of those who arrived. There was no other reaction on the part of the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as I understand what you've said, the ones who were to leave stayed for three months longer. So presumably for three months, there was an increase in the forces in the area, or have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the federal government's decision or the decision of the federal council, the decision on the extension of the military term was made for a number of troops. By that decision, they prolonged their military term from 12 months to 15. The border of the FRY was closely monitored by the mission, and no soldiers could pass without being noticed. In that light, I can responsibly claim here that the number of soldiers was not increased, it was just that the people who were doing their military term who remained a bit longer. It would have been established by the verifiers that, or rather, the verifiers would have established anything that would go to the contrary, and we would have received their objection or protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that while the new ones were being trained after arriving, the ones who had been there remained for an extra three months and that therefore both lots were there at the same time? Or have I misunderstood that? Forget the justification; just tell me the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honour, on the same day, the first group left Kosovo. They went to Merdare, and that road was used to link Serbia and Kosovo. And the other group came from Merdare to Kosovo. So the replacement happened in one day, so at no time there was an increase in numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies the position. Thank you. Now, Mr. Ackerman, now I'm trying to allow for an hour for each of two more counsel, and I know you didn't even want the length of time you already had. So how are we going to deal with this? I know you've been brief but I made a plan according to what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm nearly finished but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, carry on, but others are going to lose and I take it that's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Part of my time has been Judge's questions, which I hope you allow for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, but they didn't start until your 15 minutes were up, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your statement you state that Generals Pavkovic and General Lukic had regular contacts with Sainovic and that you knew that because when you would report something to Sainovic, he would tell you he already knew about it. My question is, did you know that Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski also had direct and regular contacts with Sainovic and were reporting things to him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, Mr. Sainovic met Mr. Drewienkiewicz on two occasions. Mr. Ciaglinski was present there alongside Mr. Drewienkiewicz. I don't know what the agenda was for the day, but in any case there were two such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. Thank you, Mr. Loncar, you have answered that question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there were also telephone contacts between them. It wasn't just meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement you described General Pavkovic as a capable military leader. I'm wondering if -- if you had occasion while you were there to make any judgements about the professional conduct of Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic; and if so, what was that judgement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I have known General Pavkovic since his student years at the military academy, that is 1966. By chance I know him exceptionally well and I can state freely that he's an exceptional professional and a military leader, an exceptional general. As for Lazarevic, I can state what most other officers of the VJ believe, that this is a general par excellence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one final question: Do you have any knowledge of the KLA ever having shot down or shot at a helicopter containing first aid markings, Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge. I know that they opened fire at regular helicopters without the sign of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, general Loncar. My name is Dan Ivetic and I am one of the attorneys for representing Sreten Lukic in these proceedings. The first area of questioning that question I have for you relates to a topic that Mr. Ackerman touched upon in your testimony, where you claim that there was regular reporting going between Generals Pavkovic and Lukic on the one hand and Mr. Sainovic on the other hand. Now, I believe you testified that it was General Lukic -- General Lukic was obliged to report to Mr. Sainovic any major incidents. Now, did any -- did this obligation arise by way of some specific legislative act, meeting, or order? I mean, please enlighten me.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic organised and planned the work of all the structures involved in Kosovo and Metohija since he was familiar with the area. As a member of the cabinet and the president of the Federal Commission, he was of the opinion that he had to be informed of everything, especially incidents. Therefore, the communication between General Lukic, Pavkovic, and Lazarevic, by way of informing Mr. Sainovic, was governed by the principle that those most responsible and well-versed in the individual parts of the terrain informed them so that they could forward that information to Mr. Sainovic himself so that he could have an insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction for the transcript. Page 28, lines 2 and 3. The witness said that Sainovic organised the work in a way so as to be able to gather information. It is missing, and in the second row or the third row it says: "Since he was familiar with the area." What the witness meant was that he organised in such a way as to be able to collect information, and perhaps we can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that what you actually said, Mr. Loncar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, so that he could gather information. He put things in that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for having to intervene again the witness said not only daily incidents and it appears as Judge Bonomy having said that. It has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General Loncar, this Federal Commission for cooperation that was established by the organs of Yugoslavia that you describe at paragraph 14 of your statement, you actually identify members of this commission, including Vlajko Stojiljkovic the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. Am I correct that this commission as a whole was meant to function so that all members were to provide the information necessary for the head of the commission, Mr. Sainovic, to be sufficiently apprised of the events relating to the OSCE in Kosovo and Metohija ? Sir, is that correct, that the members of the Federal Commission that you identify at paragraph 14 of your statement, including the minister of the interior Vlajko Stojiljkovic, were meant to communicate and pass along information to the head, Mr. Sainovic, to keep him apprised?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept or the idea behind the foundation of the federal council can be deducted from the people appointed. They were supposed to cover all spheres of life and work in Kosovo. Mr. Sainovic was the president of the commission and a cabinet member, and his idea was to ensure that one person from each of the ministries and other structures be involved, and they were supposed to inform Mr. Sainovic. For example, the representative for the internal affairs had to inform him of such affairs between the two sessions. The role was or the idea was to inform all the commission members, and I was to inform them as to the growth in strength of the mission, the method used, where the problems were, et cetera. I always took part in their meetings, and I informed the entire commission as well as Mr. Sainovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You said that the representative for internal affairs had to inform him of such affairs between the two sessions. Am I correct that for a majority of the time, both Minister of the Interior Stojiljkovic and Mr. Sainovic were based in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Pristina and Kosovo, I heard or saw him maybe once or twice, as regards Mr. Stojiljkovic. As for Sainovic, I said that he used to come once or twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When -- when they were not in Kosovo, both were in Belgrade. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Or somewhere else, but not in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that this information that you talked about, the -- where the representative for internal affairs had to inform Mr. Sainovic of things between sessions, is it your understanding that this took place on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how that daily relations worked between Mr. Stojiljkovic and Mr. Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, that answers the question. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at paragraphs 29 and 30 of your statement, sir, you described meetings that were held every Tuesday in Belgrade among the commission members, where the MUP minister Stojiljkovic gave reports and information to Sainovic. You never saw Sreten Lukic at any of these regular meetings in Belgrade, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw either Lukic or Pavkovic or Lazarevic, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Therefore, wouldn't you agree with me that it is just as logical that any information Sainovic already had when you talked with him could have come directly from Minister Stojiljkovic, and not via Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could presume that, but what I said and what I know there was in practice was that any important incidents upon Sainovic's request, Lukic had to inform him first and then to report to Stojiljkovic, who was his superior. That was the line of reporting. As for any other possibilities, well, I cannot exclude them of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say you know that this was the practice. How do you know it? Again, I asked you previously if there was any order, act of the legislature, act of the commission establishing this practice. How is it that you know of this practice that you claim was in place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Kosovo for the first time on the 12th of November, in the presence of Mr. Sainovic, in General Lukic's office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer; it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, just a moment. The interpreter has not heard that answer. I'm sorry about this, but could you start the answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood. When I went for the first time to Kosovo and Metohija with Mr. Sainovic on the 12th of November, at General Lukic's office, we saw him and General Pavkovic. Mr. Sainovic introduced me to them, and he told them I was a member of the Federal Commission and he explained my tasks. He said that all liaising between them and the OSCE should go through me, and that the practice should stay in place; that should there be any important incidents, they should report to him and -- by phone. Loncar, that is me, was to get that information from you as well and to forward it to the OSCE. That is how I realised that there had been a daily routine in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You never witnessed any reports being made in that manner, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know how they communicate; Pavkovic and Lukic, or Lukic and Sainovic, and Pavkovic and Sainovic. All I know is when I would call Mr. Sainovic to tell him something, he would say, "I already have that information." It must mean that it had been reported to him previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But you don't know by whom it had been reported to him, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As stipulated, General Lukic was to report to him any police -- as regards any police matters, and General Pavkovic any army matters, or someone from their respective office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir that Minister of the Interior Stojiljkovic in Belgrade was privy to and received daily reports from all the various MUP structures in the field directly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I hear this now, but it strikes me as something regular and normal. The minister in charge of the police needed to be apprised of any police matters in the field, although I didn't know it until now. This principle would also have to have a chain of command and some type of subordination in place to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I correct that your entire professional history and background was spent in the military, and that you have no experience within the civilian police structures of either Federal Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like to turn to the role of Colonel Mijatovic, whom you mention as being one of the individuals who worked with you in the arm of the commission in Pristina dealing with police matters. With respect to Colonel Mijatovic, you do not recall a single incident where Colonel Mijatovic refused to attend a meeting you had scheduled, do you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely never. He was always fair and attended whenever a meeting was convened by myself or the OSCE. He was never absent, not a single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So then would you be surprised to learn that Colonel Ciaglinski of the KVM claimed as part of his testimony here that "whilst Mijatovic was the MUP representative at the commission, he would rarely appear." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ciaglinski talked about a number of meetings that Mr. Loncar was not present at. So I think the question needs to be considered in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the use of the term "rarely" implies a complete different set of circumstances than is being presented by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. You need to relate your question to meetings that Mr. Loncar was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, during the meetings that you were at and that you chaired in Pristina between yourself and Colonel Ciaglinski, was there ever a meeting where Colonel Mijatovic failed or refused to appear, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said - and I can reiterate - that Mr. -- Colonel Mijatovic never as much as tried to refuse to attend any meetings convened by myself; however, I wanted to clarify this, as His Honour is right. There were two levels of meetings; one convened by myself, and the meetings convened by Colonel Kotur and Colonel Mijatovic. One for the army, the other for the police. Colonel Mijatovic had daily meetings with Mr. Mijatovic. As for Mr. Ciaglinski, he had daily contact with Colonel Kotur; and that such meetings between the two of them, there was no need for Mijatovic to be there. The same goes for the meetings of Mijatovic and Guy, there was no need for Ciaglinski to be there. One needs to understand their relations, and Mr. Mijatovic never tried not to attend any of the meetings convened by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ivetic, we should read the beginning of line 18 as "Guy."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe, either Mr. Sands or Guy. I'm not sure what came through on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these daily meetings that Colonel Mijatovic had with Mr. Sands - I believe at the time he was also a colonel - at paragraphs 28 and 31 of your statement, you describe how you received daily reports from Colonel Mijatovic regarding what had been discussed at these meetings with Mr. Sands, and you forwarded these to Walker. At paragraph 35 of your statement, you further describe that these reports were thorough and that the KVM was well-informed about all incidents. Now, what I would like to know from you is were these reports received from Mijatovic in written form or were they oral?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The oral form was unacceptable. The reports I received from Colonel Mijatovic, regarding police matters, were typed and stamped and registered. They were with the police archives and in my archives, which I later turned over to the federal archives. Therefore, it was typed, registered, and stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in general how, what length these daily reports were? Are we talking about one page? Several pages? A book?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes a single page if there were few incidents. Sometimes even up to 27. If I remember well, one report contained 31 incidents, and it had three pages. Therefore, depending on the number of incidents and the description, it could be one, two, or three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in addition to these regular meetings with yourself where Colonel Mijatovic was present, these regular and daily meetings with -- between Colonel Mijatovic and Mr. Guy Sands, do you recall a also at each regional and municipal level of the MUP structure, a MUP officer was assigned to act as a direct liaison to the KVM to be in daily contact with them regarding events that occurred within that locality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was my position that I presented to the MUP, and they agreed to it. We accepted the OSCE mission's division of Kosovo in the four sectors. They had their people covering respective areas. We followed that structure for our police, military, and administrative matters; and, therefore, in each of the sections, there was someone to liaise with the OSCE from the ranks of the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've reached the stage of our first break, which will be until 9.50, ten minutes to 10.00. We'll then sit for another 90 minutes till 11.20 and have a half-hour break and resume at 11.50 and sit until 1.00. That means that the cross-examination will need to be concluded in the next session. So you can work out your scheme accordingly, but that allows roughly the time that you each were looking for and it leaves the final session for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be doable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll resume at ten minutes to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can resume now, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Loncar, we've been talking about these daily reports that were sent to the OSCE-KVM mission about events that had already happened. But at paragraph 43 of your statement, you also indicate that the OSCE was informed of all anti-terrorist operations in advance of such operations, including Racak on 15 January 1999. I take it then that in addition to the daily reports covering events that had already occurred that there was also significant communication between at least the MUP and the KVM relating to operations that were being anticipated. Is this correct? Does this comport with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is obviously a technical problem with the microphone at Belgrade. We did not hear that answer. Just hold on, Mr. Loncar, until we are sure that the microphone is working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was our obligation to announce our activities and movements, and we did it regularly and always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you who it was that notified the Racak operation in advance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody then mentioned Racak, and nobody knew that Racak would happen. An activity was notified that would probably be a response to a prior incident. The monitors were there. It was probably an activity that was ongoing; and in the framework of that, Racak happened. Racak was never notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, that clarifies the position. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on. Now, in addition to all these meetings and contacts between Mijatovic and Guy Sands of the KVM, am I correct also that a General Richard Heaslip of the KVM was also assigned to liaise directly with General Lukic of the MUP staff? [Interpretation] In B/C/S, it would be General Heaslip?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Heaslip, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself know or verify any situation where General Lukic failed to cooperate with any requested communication on the part of the KVM, or did General Lukic cooperate fully with them, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were no special requests for anyone in the OSCE mission for any contacts or meetings with General Lukic, although there was one meeting once between General Drewienkiewicz and General Lukic. General Lukic was very diligent in that particular activity. He never refused a request. On the contrary, I know first-hand that he even insisted through Colonel Mijatovic on maximum cooperativeness in relations with the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: General, I'd next like to ask you about a matter you might remember relating to Malisevo. Do you recall any discussions that were forwarded to the commission in Belgrade relating to a request on the part of the KVM to decrease the police presence in the town of the Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that request well, and I participated in its forwarding. And the decision -- I don't remember what it was. I remember that the request was not met, because Malisevo was a key location for the KLA. They were very anxious about it, and Malisevo would have provided them with the strategic advantage in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to clear up one other matter. At paragraph 76 of your statement and, again, in your testimony these past two days, you have mentioned efforts to create what you call multi-ethnic police forces to protect villagers from the KLA. Now, are you actually aware that these so-called local security formations in these villages were in fact established and run by the municipal civilian authorities within the municipalities, rather than by the MUP, and that they were not a part of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those multi-ethnic police forces had no point of contact with MUP forces or the police. Those were forces that were supposed to encourage people to stay where they were at their homes, to continue living and working there while protecting them, but it was neither the army nor the police. They were precisely from that community. It was a body of the local authorities, not the army or the police. And their purpose was to encourage and protect the inhabitants of any given area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honour, page 39, line 11, he said, "neither the police or the army or the republic or federal authorities." The latter two are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, General, are you aware of the fact that these formations, this local security, had actually a completely different uniform from that of either the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite honestly, there were civilian parts of the clothing with military trousers and caps. They could wear blue worker's overalls. They were not uniformly dressed like the army and the police; it was just, conditionally speaking, a military set of clothing for those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sounds like a rag-tag and bob-tail operation. Was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, because there was no standard uniform for them. It was mostly like some sort of uniform of civilian protection; worker's blue overalls, shirts, jackets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, at paragraph 57 of your statement, you describe a diplomatic issue that arose at the Djeneral Jankovic crossing concerning the KVM bringing in some boxes. If I can refresh your recollection, did this have to do with credible information from the state security, the RDB, that there was a possibility of weapons being brought in by the KVM in their diplomatic pouches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In dealing with this case, I was involved, plus Mr. Mihalj Kertes, Director of the Customs Administration, and Mr. Rade Markovic was involved. He was head of the State Security Service. We went there based on a report, based on information that there was smuggling of weapons through the OSCE mission. The customs post at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing towards Macedonia said the vehicle used by General Drewienkiewicz contained two wooden cases, and we were instructed to go there and find out what it was all about. We went there. It was ordered to open the boxes, and we found a set of military binoculars but there was, in fact, no ammunition, no weaponries. In fact, there were night-sights and binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, am I correct that this issue arose and was handled by the -- by Mr. Kertes that you talked about, the Federal Customs Directorate, that they had priority over this incident as it involved customs and the Vienna Convention on consular relations?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly that it was mostly the customs administration that dealt with it. I was there because Mr. Walker and Mr. Drewienkiewicz insisted that I should be there. I don't know whether representatives of any other country were there. I know I was there, Mr. Kertes, and Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, at paragraph 59 of your statement, you describe how the relations between the KVM and the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, changed after William Walker gave his first report to the UN Security Council. First of all, sir, could you clarify, did the relations change for the better or for the worse after Mr. Walker's report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of our work and the initial good-will on both sides, our side and the OSCE mission, gave good results. And we did our best to implement the agreement from the viewpoint of our obligations towards the OSCE. And it was a constant effort invested by army and the police forces and everybody else in Kosovo to show our good-will to the international community to resolve all problems peacefully. And we expected justly, from that report, a certain expression of optimism and a recognition that we were giving our contribution to that. However, we found that that report was defeating. I personally was insulted and I felt short-selled, and others felt that, too. And our relations became, conditionally speaking, tense; however, we got over it. And we decided to intensify our work and maximise our efforts towards the OSCE with more demands and maximum engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, what was the date of that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really couldn't give you the date, but there must be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Mr. Ivetic can. Can you, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not at present, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's carry on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General Loncar, the last question I have for you: Would you agree with me that one of the main problems and points of contention during the period of the KVM mission was that various personnel, particularly within the KVM mission, had differing interpretations and understandings of the terms of the various agreements that were being verified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question, but what I experienced - and I'm not a -- I'm not a psychologist, just a soldier - but in the mission, the composition of the personnel was such that you could see from the word go, who was more inclined and had sympathy for us and who was more biased towards the Albanians. And that was not good. It's my personal conviction. And I think the mission should not have started to work until it had at least 60 or 70 percent of the envisaged personnel. I think that was one of the main and the basic reason for the failure of that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, from paragraph 59 of the statement, it would appear that the Walker report happened no later than early January 1999, although it does not have a specific date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Loncar, good morning. My name is Tomislav Visnjic, appearing for General Ojdanic. I'll ask you some questions that mainly are related to documents. I have provided the registrar in Belgrade with certain documents, and I would like him to show you 3D411.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please have on e-court 3D411, page 4 in English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Before I start my cross-examination, I would like to ask you: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it. Good morning, Mr. Visnjic. I would like to greet you and my commander, General Ojdanic, if that is allowed. Could you repeat, again, which page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: 3D411, page 4, the instruction of the VJ for cooperation with the missions of OSCE and NATO from October 1998.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean chapter 2? I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then could you please go back to chapter 1 and find paragraph 2. So my first question was: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. Although, I know that the army had instructions of this kind, but maybe I didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'll move to chapter 2, paragraph 1. General, in paragraph 1, we see the composition of bodies through which the Army of Yugoslavia was honouring its obligations towards the KVM; and according to this composition, bodies are designated at the level of the General Staff, the level of the 3rd Army, the level of the air force and air defence, and all the way down to the Pristina Corps, and even further down to garrison level and border battalions. My question is: This composition, as we see it on this page, is it consistent with what you found in practice when you arrived in Kosovo and Metohija? Were these indeed the bodies with which you cooperated on behalf of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- I'm sorry. I heard there was a liaison team for the mission, and I knew about the first item; namely, relations within the Ministry of Defence. I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the Army of Yugoslavia was trying throughout the tenure of the mission to increasingly institutionalise its relations with the mission to improve its success?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to page 5 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, when was this document produced by? In 1998, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In October 1998, and it was signed by the head of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia; at that time it was General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It strikes me as very odd that the witness didn't have this. This is the Bible you would expect to be operating the -- on which he would be operating the relationship. Astonishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a military document. And I think the witness explained, in the course of his earlier testimony, his own function within the team. I mean, the witness's function, not the role of the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, this is a man who is on the commission. This isn't just a man who's functioning as a -- some sort of underling in the set-up. So, anyway, it's a matter that can be addressed at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see, in the B/C/S version, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So, General, I want to ask you this: At the time when you arrived in Kosovo, in this document here, it is stated that the bodies we've just mentioned relate to the mission through the following. And I'll draw your attention to the appropriate paragraph, which is 3V in Serbian; in English, it would be 3C. In this paragraph, it is stated that beginning with the 23rd October 1998, "On a weekly basis for the previous week, the aforesaid teams shall submit reports," and then it is specified about which. So the reference is to weekly reports.
