Would I be right, General, in saying that in the initial period of your work, the Army of Yugoslavia submitted weekly reports to liaison officers and probably to your organs as well, that is the OSCE mission? What I mean is that the report went to the OSCE mission through your bodies.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I only now realise what various relationships were at the time. Only now do I understand why General Obradovic presented his view of the situation at the Federal Commission, which had nothing to do with my reports. He was working precisely on the basis of this. I was always wondering why he was presenting that information when we had already sent it through another channel. And now I understand that it was his right and obligation to report [Realtime transcript read in error "errors"] at these meetings on a weekly basis. But before these meetings of the commission, I was not actively involved, and you must be right that these weekly reports were sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a mistake. You'll see in the transcript the word on line 15 should be "report" and not "errors."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this report, it is said that, "The OSCE mission should be given information about movements of units the strength of a company or larger, unit arriving, departing, with or moving within the administrative borders of Kosovo and Metohija, and incidents in which VJ units took part, and steps taken against members of the VJ who took part in these incidents; accompanying the OSCE verification mission in the course of its activities in border areas; and taking part in investigation of the causes of the incidents involving VJ units." I don't want to read the whole paragraph. Of course, there is a whole series of other elements here, which are -- which stem from the duties given by the federal authorities to the Army of Yugoslavia that have to do with implementation of the agreement on the verification mission. General, sir, what I wanted to ask you is: Were these reports, if you did receive them in this form, contain this information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that I received, regular daily reports and all others, said that what you have just mentioned was consistently implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, now I would like to ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could look at the next exhibit, and that is Exhibit 3D409. It's an order assigning a liaison team with the OSCE and NATO missions, and the document gives the composition of this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Earlier, you mentioned Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Milorad Obradovic was the head of the liaison team of the VJ, General Staff, in the time of General Perisic and in the time of General Ojdanic throughout the time of the mission's operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit 3D458.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an order - we can see it on our monitors now - an order from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, signed by the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Momcilo Perisic. The date is the 16th of November, 1998. General, sir, my question is: Do you know that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia occasionally inspected the work of the teams and officers for liaison; and after these inspections, orders were issued creating more favourable conditions for the implementations of the tasks and assignments of the tasks relating to the mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking you whether you were aware that the work of the teams was controlled?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware that the Army of Yugoslavia - and you can see that on page 2 in paragraph 4 - prepared certain material preconditions for a more favourable and more efficient cooperation; such as suitable workspace for the contacts, a certain number of officers and soldiers familiar with foreign languages, also report forms, and other essential measures in order to make the work easier, both for the Army of Yugoslavia and the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they put in a lot of effort to have quality work done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 1, again, please, page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you, General, to confirm or deny, if you can, whether in the initial period of the work of the KVM, the Army of Yugoslavia realised its relations with the mission through the appropriate organs as it was announced, and only in exceptional situations and with the approval of the superior command liaison officers, independently mediated in the verification of certain activities. I'm talking about the 16th of November, 1998; that's the period.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, all the activities of the army in this area that had to do with the cooperation with OSCE considered -- and was informed about through Kotur after when the general came, who was the assistant for logistics - I can't remember his name - who was assigned -- yes, General Mladenovic, who was assigned by the 3rd Army as the main bearer of the OSCE cooperation team. That was when I actually saw what you're talking about in its full measure. Until that time before he was appointed, I had already started in early December or late November. In early December, actually, when he arrived, I learned about all of these documents, inspections. He told us what they were doing and how they were doing, and I can say that we coordinated also some matters and some positions that had to do with the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would just like to note that in paragraph 1 of this document, it also says that prior notification of inspection of VJ weapons or units, which does not comply with the provisions of the agreement on the work of the OSCE or NATO verification mission in Kosovo-Metohija, would be rejected. And this was signed by General Momcilo Perisic on the 16th of November, 1998. General, I would now like to show you Exhibit P503, and I would like you to look at page 3 of that document. I apologise. It was document P504. Can you please look at page 3 in Serbian, and it is page 4 in English. General, did Ambassador Walker ask you to pass on or insist in a different way that cooperation with representatives of the Army of Yugoslavia be improved, by asking them to submit daily reports and establish daily contacts, as is stated in this document? We're talking about the last sentence of paragraph 1, which is just above paragraph 2. I don't know if you found that.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have. It says: "In addition, Loncar accepted Walker's assessment that the cooperation between the KVM and the KDOM is satisfactory and well-established, and that the same kind of cooperation should be continued with representatives of the Yugoslav army (the submission of daily reports and the establishment of daily contacts)." Mr. Visnjic, relating to the question of whether we knew of the contents of the agreement for the inspection and monitoring of weaponry, I had the opportunity at a meeting with General Drewienkiewicz, who sought to inspect the facilities of a brigade, and he referred to General Ojdanic's agreement, who was at the time the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Then I arranged a meeting and he confirmed that this was part of the agreement, but he said that he did not agree or approve that General Drewienkiewicz to go into a brigade and monitor their weaponry, so on and so forth. This is what we knew and this is what he adhered to. As for this question, I affirm that the cooperation was good, and the army agreed to start sending daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, General, but we seem to have last track in the interpretation. My colleague says that the entire interpretation - and this is page 50 or something - the whole translation that starts from page 50, line 14 to line -- to page 50, line 25 has actually a little bit slipped up. So I would like to put the question to you again. Before you testified what the framework of the agreement was and what the rights of the verifiers were, my first question is: Whether the Army of Yugoslavia ever had the habit of interpreting international agreements?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to your understanding, is the Army of Yugoslavia an operative organisation, and does it implement everything that is concluded at the federal level?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is the organ that implements --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- decisions of the federal organs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as the staff is in the command, that is what the federal government is in relation to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still on this topic, and that is why I would like to ask you to look at Exhibit P506, page 2, paragraph 2. Could you please read the first few sentences of this paragraph, and then I will put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it aloud or for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, just read the text for yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you were aware that General Drewienkiewicz spoke with General Ojdanic. I don't know if you know the date, but this was on the 27th of November, the same day that General Ojdanic assumed his duties from General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Drewienkiewicz told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After that meeting, do you know - and I can see that you do know about it, based on what you said - that the General Staff team went to Kosovo with the objective of establishing the framework and the content of the future cooperation of the VJ and the KVM. Do you know that the team went there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know. And I had contacts with the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Regarding these different interpretations of the agreement that we discussed, are you aware also that the VJ asked clarification from relevant federal organs about the rights and the duties of the army and the rights and the duties of the verifiers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what General Ojdanic told me in my telephone conversation with him. In the presence of General Drewienkiewicz, we were asking for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now I would like to ask you to look at exhibit -- well, to put it in context, we are talking about the 20th of December. This conversation with Mr. Drewienkiewicz in the presence of other members, but for now let's leave that aside. So you conducted this conversation on the 21st -- no, the 20th of December, 1999 [as interpreted]. Can we now look at Exhibit 3D408. And I'm sorry, but in the transcript it should state 1998; the 20th of December, 1998. Three days after this conversation, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia issued an order signed by General Ojdanic. This was the 23rd of December, 1998. In the order, the measures are stated in detail as well as the framework of the cooperation and measures that are to be taken in order to upgrade this cooperation. This is an additional order to the instructions that we mentioned already. This is 3D411 and 3D458. General, I would like to ask you to go through the document. I will begin from some important issues - our time is limited - so let's look at paragraph 3. You said that officers who were assigned as liaison team officers, besides their regular duties, also carried out this additional duty of liaison officers. They did that on top of their regular duties. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This order, in paragraph 3, enables them to be released from a part of their regular duties so that they could devote themselves more to this assignment of being liaison officers with the KVM and to be available 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Visnjic, you don't really need to read all this out. If there's a particular question you want to ask the witness, you should go to the question. It would actually help your case much more if you were asking -- you don't have to, obviously, in cross-examination. But bearing in mind this is building a Defence case, it would be far more valuable if you asked him questions and we got spontaneous answers, rather than lead him by the nose through documents just to nod his head in response to your assertion of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have already asked the question. I can't go back, but I'll try this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, was it the intent that liaison officers should be available 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this did not happen on the 23rd. It happened a few days later. Kotur came from the command where he was based. He would only come just before meetings or in the morning to meet Ciaglinski and told me that this order had come in. And I remember this because he was a specifically designated officer for contacts with the OSCE, and this man was specifically designated as liaison officer for border battalions. And he was always involved whenever border incidents were discussed. So I know that these officers were specifically tasked to deal with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to paragraph 4. Is it the case that at some point the Army of Yugoslavia started submitting daily reports to the OSCE mission, in keeping with the request of Mr. Walker and in keeping with your discussions with General Drewienkiewicz and Mr. Walker, from the 20th of December, and a prior meeting of the 16th of December?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't wait for that order. I thought it was necessary. It needed to be done, as soon as we started contacting with the mission. And the order just confirmed that this is the way it should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This decision also specified the framework of verification, which, unlike the previous order from General Perisic, specified that verifiers also have the right to inspect units outside barracks, which was not said in the previous document. But equally some restrictions were placed on them consistent with earlier restrictions made by Perisic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was a very good framework that left no room for any dilemmas or any inclarities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: One of the problems was that a certain number of designated liaison officers did not speak English. To what extent did this complicate the work of liaison teams?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A great deal, a great deal. I felt it personally. My lack of English resulted in longer meetings, and I felt handicapped on all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago that an officer, a liaison officer was designated for the border belt who became a permanent member of the team. Is that consistent with what is written in paragraph 5 of this order? And I mean --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is completely consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The activities of border units guarding the state border?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 3D408. [In English] Pardon, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] 3D407, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the period following this order, or let's say from the end of year 1998 until this order in 1999, I suppose that you had gained some experience, and some deficiencies in your work had been observed. Tell me, General, was the framework of cooperation constantly improved? Were there any attempts to address problems and deficiencies or to alleviate them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the very nature of those activities, it is normal that from the beginning we need to put certain things on track and activities constantly improved. The number of verifiers increased. We had gained more experience with time; and just in the normal course of things, our relations in cooperation with the OSCE improved day by day. And that continued until the first report submitted by Walker, then there was a brief stag nation, and then it returned back on track, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer. He's speaking too fast, constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, if I can interrupt for a moment. Mr. Loncar, the interpreter is asking you to speak a little more slowly, if you can. And, Mr. Visnjic, please wait until the answer is finished on the transcript before you start your question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, and I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this order of the 8th of March, 1999 was signed by General Ojdanic. It sets out a new structure of the teams of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the last page of the document. Your Honour, in order to avoid going through the entire document, I will tender it later. But the last page shows a schematic of VJ liaison teams, and I would ask the witness to comment upon it based on questions I will ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like the first schematic we've seen to be found in the order of General Perisic from October 1998 titled, "Instruction," 3D411. I see that in this schematic, the teams of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps were integrated into one. What is your explanation for this, for this reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that higher quality of relations was achieved in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question has to do with the composition of liaison teams. And in the right bottom corner - I don't know if you can see it well in your copy - but we see the total number of officers, generals, and civilians. Now we have as many as three generals and 49 officers working on liaison teams. Did this number reflect an increase in the numbers of the verification mission in that time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does this number correspond to an increase in the numbers of the verifiers in the previous period?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE mission continued to be reinforced until the end of the year. After the new year, 1999, new verifiers stopped arriving and the number stopped at 1400 or 1500. Of course, the increased number of officers considerably improved our engagement and our ability to carry out specific actions, more actions, and better cooperation with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, just before you move on, one transcript point, line 6 on page 57. I was expecting it to change, but it hasn't. It should read "unlike the first schematic." Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Speaking of quality, General, is it true that these officers included in the mission, according to the new schematic, all spoke English and had passed certain vetting. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group of officers was discussed with the previous counsel. Mr. Drewienkiewicz had a meeting with that new group of officers, who had very good English, and briefed them about the situation in Kosovo from the viewpoint of the OSCE mission. I can really say that it was a new quality, indeed, but they arrived to late in Kosovo in my opinion. Because just after they arrived, the mission threatened to leave. The possibility of bombing was mentioned more and more often in public, and that new group of officers did not have time to make a contribution because of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On page 3 of this order, it is ordered to prepare new liaison officers through a workshop to be held on the 15th of March, 1999. And that is precisely the workshop that you mentioned, responding to the questions of my colleague Mr. Cepic. That workshop was attended by both you and General Drewienkiewicz. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there the whole time; whereas, General Drewienkiewicz visited only when he gave his presentation and answered the questions of the attending officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one related question based on a document. Never mind. We'll move on. General, I'd like to go through a couple of documents together with you. We have a whole series of documents, in fact. Could you please look at 3D459. It is a report of the liaison team of the 3rd Army command sent to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia to the General Staff's liaison team. General, about these reports that went through military channels, did you receive them in this form, or were you informed, as you described, directly by representatives of the army in your team?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not in this format; but if I look at the content, it's the same as what we had. But we had a different format for writing reports that was prescribed for both the MUP and the army for easier reporting to the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to say about the format that the general is talking about, it is to be found on the last page of 3D408. It's an integral part of the order to be found in Exhibit 3D408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Visnjic. I'm becoming confused. This one that's on the screen at the moment is a daily report to the liaison team, but the witness has just said he didn't get this. So I'm struggling to understand what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I explain or do you want the witness to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you try to explain to me, and we'll see if we need his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 3rd Army had its own liaison team for cooperation with the mission, and that team sent reports to the General Staff's team. So in addition to direct reporting to Colonel Kotur and General Loncar at the level of Kosovo, there was parallel reporting directly to the General Staff through military channels. But what I wanted to ask General Loncar is whether the content of the documents was similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rather, the pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at some of the events described here; for instance, a border incident in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, I would like to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, as a member of the Federal Commission and the main man in cooperation with the OSCE, I was not at all interested in your military reports that you sent through the chain of command that describe the situation. I was only interested in reports from the Pristina Corps concerning the territory of Kosovo and Metohija that I received every morning from Colonel Kotur. And that was the channel: Pristina Corps to the Federal Commission, and through the Federal Commission to the OSCE. And this was the reporting within our own structures regarding military knowledge from the lowest-level observer to the highest organs. Otherwise, all the issues covered here were covered in my reports. And, as I said, the army and the police had a slightly modified report that I submitted to the mission every morning. I wanted just to explain this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, what do you then understand that this document on the screen actually is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, in my view, is an order and a form of reporting about incidents from the Kosovo and Metohija area to the army structures; and on the basis of that, analysis were made and appropriate measures are decided on in relation to the incidents. So it had to do with military subordination. I, as a member of the commission of a political organ or body, received the same thing but in a different form from the Pristina Corps, and I would send that on to the mission. So according to me, this was a form of a report intended for military structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not put any more questions to the witness on this document or a whole series of documents that I had, because he's already answered the question. But I would like to ask two more questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are going to go back to what you talked about with my colleague, Mr. Cepic. My colleague, Mr. Cepic, put some questions to you about General Drewienkiewicz's statements and the statements by Colonel Ciaglinski. Both used the word "manoeuvres." General, regular training at the level of a platoon or a company, can that be considered a manoeuvre?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to the military terminology, the term should be "viewed" in the context in which it was applied. In our conditions,, manoeuvres imply the engagement, the training, and the movement of units of a strategic level; whereas, platoon, a company, a battalion are tactical units. So, the term manoeuvre is inappropriate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the time you were in Kosovo and at the time the KVM was there, did the Pristina Corps at any time conduct exercises and manoeuvres in the area 20 by 20 kilometres, which would also include a large number of Albanian villages and the closing off of access?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A corps does not carry out manoeuvres. A corps also conducts tactical, joint exercises of an operational level. So it's not correct that a corps can execute manoeuvres, at least in our military terminology. Secondly, any movements of units of the Pristina Corps from a section upwards was announced to the KVM, and we adhered strictly to the provisions of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski at meetings with you ever said that there were more than 15 companies outside of barracks in Kosovo, which would constitute a violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always their effort to pass on their request that units outside of the barracks be returned to the barracks; however, I explained to them that the agreement provided for the deployment outside of barracks of four combat groups. This was entered in all the maps and provided as an annex to the agreement. These are four combat groups, the strength of four reinforced companies, and not the number that they used, that you mentioned. So only four combat groups were deployed outside the barrack facilities, and this was in accordance with the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And one question that is not directly related to this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on to that then. I don't know if the earlier question was actually answered. Mr. Loncar, were there circumstances where a training exercise involved closing off access to villages inhabited by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The combat groups, the four combat groups could only execute movements and use a limited area, which was specified on the map and in the field. They did not go beyond those approved sectors. They did not perform exercise activities outside. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And finally, one question, General, that is not directly related to the topic of Kosovo. At a certain point in your career, you worked together with General Ojdanic. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what your opinion is of him as an officer.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to inform the members of the Trial Chamber that I was in the Uzice Corps as Chief of Staff, and my commander was General Ojdanic. So I was his first associate or I was deputy corps commander. General Ojdanic left to become the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army, and I assumed his duties in the Uzice Corps. Other than those two, three years of work together, I have known General Ojdanic since 1961 or 1962. We had an identical career, it was similar; and I can only say the best of General Ojdanic and the awards and recognition he has received affirm his qualities and his good work. I was on particularly good terms with the family of Mr. Ojdanic. It's a very honourable and good family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hannis, is the final session going to be sufficient for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, I wonder if we could take our break now and finish ten minutes earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we do that, I want to ask if Mr. Cepic wants his other five minutes in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loncar, my colleague, Mr. Visnjic, asked you about the deployed units which, in keeping with the agreement, were on certain locations to protect roads. You probably know that there were also nine combat groups were in-depth security of the border and the verification mission knew their coordinates and visited them in the border area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But those were units that were on specific locations, and only if necessary would they be engaged according to a particular decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just one correction, if you accept it. Is it the case that there were, in fact, three companies deployed in locations; Dulje, Lapusnik, and Volujak according to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it was three or four, I don't know after such time. But there is a document that we could look up. It could have been three or four, but the document specifies exactly how many and where they were deployed in accordance with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: Do you know if there was any plan ever to attack the civilian Albanian population and expel them from the area of Kosovo and Metohija? Did such a plan ever exist, General?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, knowing the people at the head of that corps, General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, and all the chief commanders and heads of organs, I would exclude any kind of possibility in that sense, and I think that that would be highly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Well, in that case we will take the break now and we will resume again at 20 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can again resume the hearing. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, yesterday Mr. Fila asked you some questions about Mr. Sainovic and where he got his authority from for his job with the Federal Commission. At page 7585, line 15, in your answer you said: "Anything he did within the commission was within the part of his duties as the deputy prime minister, based on the task and position he received from the federal government." And on the next page, 7586, in another answer where you talked about, "sometimes Sainovic was not able to give an answer immediately and he had to pass those demands on. He had to consult the federal government." In those two contexts, General, who was the federal government? The federal government as made up of individual persons. What persons did Mr. Sainovic get his authority from to do the work on the Federal Commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one correction. It's a slip. He wasn't deputy minister, but he was the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the federal government, the executive organs are -- consist of ministers, and they, together with the prime ministers, the deputy prime ministers, make up the government. Mr. Sainovic was the deputy prime minister. He didn't have an executive function like the ministers did. His activities and implementation of decisions, orders arose from the powers of the government. The government had to make the decision and then transfer the authority to him for him to implement those decisions. So that is how Mr. Sainovic would be able to provide an answer to some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: What person or persons gave him that power? What person or persons told him what answers he could give to the KVM verifiers? It had to be some individual persons.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of a state is a collective decision by the government, which is headed by the prime minister. At the time, it was Mr. Bulatovic; that is why I conclude that he was the prime minister. Based on the government of -- based on the decision of the government; thus, it was Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't it a fact that in connection with the work of the Federal Commission that Mr. Bulatovic would have also taken direction or instruction from Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in all countries of the world, regardless of the social order, whether it's a monarch, an emperor, a president, and so on and so forth, he would be the most prominent political person and, of course, would have the influence to a greater or lesser degree on the position and the work of the government. So it would be normal to expect that the president of the state had an influence on the decision of the government -- on the decisions of the government, which in my view is quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with you, it's quite normal. Would you agree that that was the case in the former Yugoslavia at that time, in 1998, that Mr. Milosevic would have had that power and exercised that influence?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late president was well-known for his dynamic work and his activities, which means he was probably abreast of the events and had an influence on the work of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that connection in paragraph 14 of your statement, you talk about when Mr. Milosevic asked you to meet with him about working on the Federal Commission; and in the last sentence of that paragraph you say: "Since Milosevic wanted me on this council, he said he would instruct Bulatovic to include me." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he used the term "instruct," but the gist comes down to this, that he would contact Bulatovic and indicate to him to include me in the Federal Commission. I don't know if I used the adequate term, but it was said that he would contact Bulatovic, and he would present to him the need to include me in the composition of the Federal Commission. So I assume that it would be so that in the contacts with Walker, there would be some sort of relationship established; and he could get some points on account of me, because Mr. Walker had expressed the desire to work with me in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 68, line 10, suggested that I be "included" and here it says "indicated." The witness said, "to suggest to Bulatovic to include him in the work of the commission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result, after that meeting you were appointed to the commission, yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila then, at page 7589, asked you whether or not Mr. Sainovic was just the first among equals and whether or not he had greater powers than you. You said in some missions, in some tasks, you had more responsibility than him. Let me ask you this: At the Federal Commission meetings in Belgrade or any meetings that Mr. Sainovic chaired in Pristina, who chaired those meetings? Who led those meetings when Mr. Sainovic was present?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the meetings were held between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Walker, the meetings were chaired by Mr. Sainovic on our side and by Mr. Walker on the side of the OSCE. In view of the fact that Mr. Sainovic knew English very well, the dialogue between those two figures proceeded in the English language. I always had an interpreter next to me who translated their dialogue to me into Serbian. The meeting was chaired by Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the weekly meetings in Belgrade of the commission, just you Serbian members of the commission, who chaired those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meetings when the work was analysed and the results of the work of the Federal Commission, which was always held in Mr. Sainovic's office, Mr. Sainovic would be the one to chair the meeting or to conduct the meeting, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you indicated to us that Mr. Sainovic would give instructions, specific instructions to some of the other members of the commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Let me use my own example. When I suggested on the second meeting of the Federal Commission that it would be rational to form five lower-ranking teams in the territory of Kosovo, lower-ranking in relation to mine and what their composition would be - and there was some other proposals brought out also by other members of the commission - and in the end when Mr. Sainovic took the floor and said, "What you suggested, General, was very good and you can start to implement that." So in that context, he did issue specific assignments to certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anybody else in the group assign tasks, other than Mr. Sainovic, during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one assigned tasks. Mostly they were ministers from the federal government. In a way, in their briefings, they acquainted the other members who were not members of the federal government, like me, Mr. Kertes, General Obradovic, not to mention any others, what he as a minister was given as an assignment relating to duties in Kosovo and Metohija. So, indirectly, they stated their assignments and acquainted everybody else with their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 7598, line 11, from yesterday, Judge Bonomy asked you a question regarding the request for a helicopter from Mr. Walker. And you had indicated that this was a cabinet decision and not something that Mr. Sainovic had the right to make himself. Do you know -- well, how do you know that the question about the helicopter was a decision for the cabinet, instead of Mr. Sainovic as president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to try my best to remember this relation between Mr. Sainovic and me when he more or less told me -- I think I'm right to say that he said, "General, when the helicopter is in question, please tell me Mr. Walker that it has been decided not to approve bringing the helicopter from Switzerland, but if they would like I'm -- we are going to provide our own helicopter and they can adapt that to their needs." So I think that is the suggestion. I think he addressed me with the term -- I don't think he addressed me with the term "I decided," but it was decided. So I think, Judge, this was an indication that this decision had come from a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer yesterday at page 7599, lines 4 you said the gist of what Mr. Sainovic responded was that this was not something provided for in the agreement, and he said, "He would pass it on to the proper authorities and get a reply." Who would have been the proper authorities for that question, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal government headed by the prime minister, Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to some questions that Mr. Cepic asked you. At page 7611, yesterday Mr. Cepic asked you about whether or not the army commanded the MUP or the MUP commanded the army. You said while you were there neither one, neither the MUP commanded the army nor the army commanding the MUP. General, do you know during this -- during a state of war or one of the three extraordinary states in the former Yugoslavia, was there a provision whereby for combat activities the MUP was to be subordinated to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honourable Judge, our rules and regulations provide precisely what you say was applied in those three extraordinary situations. And it clarifies if in a given area a large number of MUP forces are situated and they are the bearers of combat actions and there is a lower-ranking unit there, then the army is subordinated to the police and the other way around, but always the case was that there were more soldiers and policemen. But the practice that is always -- that is the practice that is always applied in accordance with our positive military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, that sounds logical. In your answer yesterday, you went on at page 7613 at lines 3 and lines 17, to say that: "As for combat activities, a full cooperation was needed between the two armed components of the state. It was necessary and indispensable." Were you aware of the existence of a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija during the time that you were in Kosovo in late 1998 and early 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this goes far beyond the framework of the cross-examination, this term, this institution referred to has not been mentioned in any of the cross-examinations. Therefore, I believe it is inappropriate for the Prosecutor to introduce it now, trying to put forth new evidence in this phase of this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the questions about whether or not MUP was in charge or VJ was in charge, cooperation, coordination, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll repel the objection. We are satisfied that coordination of operations was an issue in cross-examination, and it's appropriate to re-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Generally speaking, as for your question, I can reply in a general way. Of course the effect of joining the police and police forces is far better if coordination is sufficient and good and if the forces are being put together. But during the activities in Kosovo, there were no Joint Commands and no joint activities. As for what was reported in the media - and I tried to follow that as a retired general - it was never mentioned that such a thing as the Joint Command was in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked a question by Mr. Cepic about something that General DZ had said in his statement. I think it's at paragraph 166 of General DZ's statement, and this was when you were sent to Rogovo in connection with an incident that happened there in late January 1999. I think Mr. Cepic asked it in terms of DZ put you in the chain of command for the MUP. His statement says, "There I saw Loncar. He was clearly in charge of the situation. He was giving orders to the police present, and they also sought instructions from him." General, when you were out there, were you talking with the police on the scene?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking to the policemen there; however, Your Honour, my primary task as a commission member and the person heading a team, as well as the duties of Mr. Walker or his assistants, were to try and be arbiters in case of incidents, to try and determine who was to blame for a given incident. Then the Rogovo incident occurred. I was called by Mr. Sainovic. I received a phone call, and he told me, "General, go there and don't allow them to ascribe the responsibility for this one as they did for Racak." I thought it was important for me to be there, and I contacted the policemen who were there in numbers, as well as many OSCE monitors. Drewienkiewicz came an hour or an hour and a half after me. In the presence of the most responsible person of the OSCE for the west, I asked him, with several witnesses standing by, to describe to me what sort of clothes the KLA terrorists wore. And he said, "They wore military uniforms." And he said, "They did." And what -- I asked what type of weapons they had, and he described them, and it was all noted down. When I asked him whether they had gone through all the verifiers and everything they had to say, they said they did. And then I tried to make use of the authority I enjoyed there, and I said, "Well, carry on with the activities." And then Mr. Drewienkiewicz came, and I guess this is what he saw me as being someone who was issuing orders and commanding, although I had no authority to do that at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Petrovic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. A correct for the transcript, page 74, line 18, it says: "Carry on with the activities." The witness said: "Carry on with the activities pertaining to the on-site investigation." That is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, DZ said in his statement that there were two different types of police out there at Rogovo. Do you recall who was there from the police and do you know which units they were with?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I heard there were two types of police in Kosovo. There was only one police; however, some of them wore their -- wore camouflage police uniforms, whereas the others wore the official regular uniform. This is what may have caused the impression with General Drewienkiewicz as having seen two types of police, but I claim that there was only one police force in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, in connection with that, were you aware of the existence of various elite or special units of the police, such as the PJP or the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew there was the so-called cobra special anti-terrorist unit in the military. As for the police, I didn't know they had any special or specialised units. I knew they all underwent intensive training in both Serbia and Kosovo to combat terrorism --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it you weren't --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I presume they drew people from those ranks. But as to whether they had ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it you weren't familiar with a state security special unit called the JSO?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it existed, but in the territory of Serbia and not in Kosovo. That unit was not in Kosovo at the time. I know of it. It was a much discussed unit in the political circles the year before, but at that time it was not present there. I know that it exists, though, but it is a security type of force rather than a force of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then today Mr. Cepic was asking you some questions, and he spoke to paragraph 49 of your statement and discussions with DZ and DZ's complaints about excessive force being used by the Serb forces. In your answer at page 2 today, line 10, you say, "The army was not deployed with tanks. It was an exercise which had been planned and announced to the OSCE and it had to do with training of the new generation of tank operators." At the end of that paragraph you say: "But it was merely by chance that the army was there at the same time, though their tanks differed." That answer doesn't seem to make sense to me. Did somebody else have tanks besides the army, or has that been mistranslated some way? You seem to be referring to the fact that both MUP and VJ were in the area at the same time.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. At the same time, in the same area, they had physical contact. We had the MUP and the army troops there. In the planning of exercises for every unit, the place is specified. And if you go through such documents you can see that exercises are being planned for a month ahead, specifying the location where the tank unit was. But it is another thing that the incident happened to -- or in the proximity of that tank unit, and then it turned out as if the army and the police were there together. But such training had been pre-planned in order to train members of the tank unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess you still haven't answered the last part of my question, though. It says: "Though their tanks differed." Whose tanks differed and in what way?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the armoured vehicles of the police differed from those of the army. Armoured vehicles, that does not include only tanks. That should include APCs, tanks, and so on and so forth. The first category is blue, the police ones; and the military ones are the olive-green-grey colour. That was the context in which I meant the tanks differed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Today at page 9 Mr. Cepic had asked you about DZ and the OSCE's request to visit -- visit facilities of the VJ. And the OSCE complained about not being able to visit the barracks, did they not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 33 of your statement, General, you say that DZ wanted to inspect facilities but Sainovic told you: "Always said it was not in the agreement or annexes." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it wasn't in the agreement or the annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Your Honour, I do apologise. I thought that the complete answer wasn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 12, line 11, today you were answering a question about the conduct of the verifiers, and you said: "We also had verifiers that observed things from a kilometre's distance but write about things as if they had been on the spot. They report things in a way that was not authentic and accurate." You're not saying that all verifiers wrote things that were not authentic and accurate, are you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I said a part of them observed things from a distance, and they feared for their lives, lacking the courage to approach, whereas some others did. So I didn't mean to include all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware, General, that in some instances when KVM verifiers tried to approach more closely areas of alleged incidents, that they were sometimes forced away at gunpoint?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I hear of this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know it was not your job, General, but apart from Rogovo, when Mr. Sainovic sent you there, did you personally go to any incident sites to see for yourself whether what KVM was reporting was accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the bombing attack of the terrorists in Pristina, I was in the area of Devet Jugovica. I was observing tank hill, as was termed here. I was also in the area of Podujevo when there were Albanian demonstrations. Therefore, I was in the field on five or six occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know you indicated that on --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something that was in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I interrupted you, General. Were you finished?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to say this: As I stated a minute ago, we had to act as arbiters in any and in every incident, and in most cases it was done at the lower level of the commission. As for Mr. Walker and myself, and Mr. Drewienkiewicz and myself, I did not receive any invitations from Drewienkiewicz to go together in the field. The first and only instance was when he called me to go to Racak together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you indicated in an answer about the daily reports you were getting from the MUP that one day you had a report with 33 incidents in it. And there simply was no way you could go out and try to confirm or verify all the reports that you were receiving from the MUP, from the VJ, and from the KVM, was there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, Mr. Loncar. Just a moment we have counsel on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps my learned friend Mr. Hannis could state the foundation for this question, to what part of testimony does this refer to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he -- he may have misquoted the figure as 33, but the witness definitely referred to a report with 31 incidents in cross-examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour it is 31 and it was at page 35, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed with your answer, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that I mentioned the figure of 31. If I recall it correctly, that was the number of incidents in a single day, but those were the incidents such as a group of terrorists barged into a house and harassed a Roma woman in the presence of her parents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, the question is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Raped a Roma woman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand you wanted to tell us some of the detail, but the question was: There simply was no way you could go out and try to verify all the reports you were receiving because of the volume of these reports. That's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is: Yes, precisely. Most of the incidents were investigated by the commission at its lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 14, line 16, today, Mr. Cepic asked you if you could say it was the KLA that instructed their own civilian population to move out or transfer somewhere else. You said: "I don't know about the cooperation between the KLA and their own ethnic Albanian population, but from the military aspect it was obvious that there was obedience and cooperation." So if I understand you correctly, it appeared that the KLA was able to operate -- to command and control their fighters, but you have no knowledge about whether or not civilians were being instructed and obeying instructions of the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, but all the incidents and activities taking place caused by the terrorists or the KLA involved no civilians. Who could have ordered civilians? The police and the army or the terrorists, forcing the people of their own ethnic background to move? What you stated is correct, but also it should be put in the wider context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You yourself didn't have an opportunity to interview any KLA commanders or any Kosovo Albanian civilians about that particular aspect, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directly as regards to that issue, no. As for the commanders, I never had occasion and I never wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman today asked you a question at page -- I think beginning at page 18, and he was referring you to something that Judge Bonomy had asked you yesterday about the KVM not referring to the KLA as terrorist. And Judge Bonomy raised the issue with you if it wasn't a possibility that one reason they didn't do that was to try and have a better relationship with them and maybe be able to dissuade them from doing certain things. Mr. Ackerman asked, "Would you agree that if that was their purpose, to improve the influence they might have on the terrorists, on the KLA, that it was a complete failure. It didn't work?" And you said -- well, your answer went on for a little bit. In the end you said: "So what you're asking me, I believe you're right, so my answer would be yes." But, General, you couldn't know about the times that KVM may have been successful in persuading KLA to either withdraw from an area or refrain from a certain action or not engage in provocations, because there wouldn't have been any action; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. I didn't know what they were doing when they went to visit the Albanian side, and they never told us of any successes in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 22, line 12, today in an answer to Mr. Ackerman, I think you said, "I must state decisively that the army, the members of the Army of Yugoslavia, and the Pristina Corps, first of all, did not conduct a single offensive action. Their activities were exclusively in response." Can I ask you: Do you know, was the army involved in, either directly or indirectly, in support of the MUP by providing artillery fire or tank fire or by simply setting up a cordon around the perimeter of an area where the MUP was carrying out activities in, first of all, Podujevo in December 1998? Was the army involved any way in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the time I was there, I had no knowledge of that. I really don't have any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No knowledge --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such coordinated activities between the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, no VJ involvement in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the army did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about on the 12th of March, 1999, in the area of Jeskovo village, an operation involving elements of the 549th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, on what day or date?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 12th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that, because at that time we were intensively trying to organise the evacuation of the OSCE mission. And they were busy with their own withdrawal as well. Therefore, I have no knowledge of this incident. I didn't even know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I need to follow-up a question regarding the -- those conscripts who had finished their 12 months and then were extended for another three months, the ones that we were calling the 15-monthers. When they stayed their additional three months, did they stay in Kosovo the entire time until their 15 months were up?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within their units. They spent all that time in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did their replacements not arrive in Kosovo until 15 months were up, or had they come at the end of 12 months?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but it's a simple question and there's -- since it does arise, the Prosecution -- from cross-examination, the Prosecutor is entitled to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only after the 15th month has expired in their military service, they were replaced by another contingent from Serbia. So the replacements did not arrive after the first 12 months but after the 15th month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then in --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence - I apologise - is that they did not spend three months together. They were not together for a single day, the two contingents. The exchange was done the same day. One contingent left Kosovo and the other one entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I was confused because I thought you indicated when -- when that replacement or that transfer or that shift occurred, that one group went to Merdare. Can you tell us where Merdare is located.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Merdare is the northern-most location. It is on the very border between Kosovo and Metohija and Serbia. Therefore, it is the northern-most location in Kosovo, the first one comes across when coming from going Serbia. It is on route from Kosovo to Serbia towards Prokuplje via Merdare, and at Merdare the Serbian contingent entered and the Kosovo one left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that since their 15 months was up, they were going home. They were leaving because they had finished their term of service; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They all went home after the completion of their military term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, were you aware of elements of the 37th Brigade being brought into Kosovo on or around the 7th of March, 1999, brought in from Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, through a combination of circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, something is missing -- oh, it's coming into the transcript now. It's just we heard something in Serbian that was not on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it affect the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can deal with it later if it still has to be dealt with. Please carry on with your answer, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So through a combination of circumstances, I was commanding the Uzice Corps or I was the Chief of Staff, and that 37th Brigade was part of the Uzice Corps and based in Racak. So it couldn't have come from Montenegro. It had never been in Montenegro. So that's one correction. And the second correction is that it was a period when the situation was already clear. It was clear that the air-strikes were coming, the situation was increasingly complex. I don't know, but if I had been commander, I would have ordered movement of that brigade that was closest to Kosovo just for prevention purposes. That is what all wise armies would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't disagree with you on that, General, but my question was: Did you know that elements of the 37th Brigade entered Kosovo on or about the 7th of March, 1999; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, nobody except the establishment of the Pristina Corps entered Kosovo. I don't think it's correct that the 37th Brigade or any of its troops entered Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Loncar, you referred to the 37th Brigade being based in Racak. Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Raska, R-a-s-k-a, that is a town in the south of Serbia. That is the establishment location of the 37th Brigade. That is in the area of Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, Mr. Ivetic, counsel for General Lukic, was asking you some questions about the multi-ethnic police forces, which he explained were actually local security and had a completely different uniform than the army or the police. Do you know what these units were called? Do you know what the name for them was?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I have to emphasise that General Lukic and his police had nothing to do with those multi-ethnic forces. Since their forces -- since their tasks in -- I know who baptised them as police forces, because I already specified those were local forces, who were there to encourage and protect the local residents as much as they could. What their name was, I don't know. I personally referred to them as local police of Kosovska Mitrovica, say, or the local police of Prizren when they were in question. They had -- they were multi-ethnic in character. That's all I can tell you. Because they were--

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who provided them their weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what they were armed with or who armed them. I mean, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In a -- well, there's been evidence to suggest that there were no paramilitaries in Kosovo. If these security forces were not under the VJ and not under the MUP, wouldn't they have been a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of your explanation and your question, yes, they would have been paramilitary. But I believed they belonged -- in fact, they were forces of security. They belonged to the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were certainly not from the police, and they were certainly not from the army. They could only have belonged to security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, in a state of emergency, state of war, or state of imminent threat of war, under the Law on Defence and other applicable laws in the former Yugoslavia at the time, under whose authority would these local security forces fall? Who would control them? Who would direct them in times of war and combat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whoever established them, because they would have been directed subordinated to the entity that established them. So they were established by the security council within the FRY, and it's probably that security council that commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if -- would these security forces then be what is referred to in Joint Command orders, in late March 1999, as the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Hannis, there's nothing wrong with the question. It's the source that just complicates it. What you're asking the witness is whether that description would fit. Is that right? Because he's denied any knowledge of any Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I guess, but I'm asking the question in connection with that because the orders direct the armory to engage the non-Siptar population -- the armed non-Siptar population. That's why I ask it in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, just a brief comment about the police that my learned friend Mr. Hannis is referring to. He's talking about the non-Albanian population. As far as I understood the testimony of this witness, it's not about non-Albanians. On the contrary, most of those people were Albanians, ethnic Albanians within those units. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, that comment may be made in due course about what this evidence amounts to. I know that Mr. Ivetic asked the questions, based upon the idea that this was an Albanian security force. But Mr. Hannis's questions come at it from a rather different angle, and he's trying to build on what emerged from the evidence in cross-examination. So there's nothing inappropriate about that. But, Mr. Ivetic, you wanted to say something else? No. The question will be allowed, but not on the basis of the Joint Command, Mr. Hannis. So you can put it differently, as I've suggested already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, were you aware of the armed non-Siptar population in Kosovo? Who would that have been that were not in the army, that was not empty MUP, that was armed, and that was non-Siptar?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be that I wasn't precise or concise enough. What I'm trying to say is that the main trend and the main effort was to set up a structure or a unit or a component, or call it what you like, of the police that would not be mainly Serb, because there was already a Serb police force commanded by General Lukic, but it was poorly accepted by Albanians. So something new needed to be created, something that would have had and enjoyed the confidence of the people, and that's how this multi-ethnic police came about. They were established at the local level, by local authorities, and most of the men were Albanians, Gorani, et cetera. So that is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Loncar, the question is rather different. We've had evidence earlier of a reference to the mobilisation of the non-Siptar population. Now, assuming that's accurate evidence, what -- just hold on until I finish the question. Assuming that's accurate evidence for the moment, to what would it be referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is a mobilisation of the Serbs going on, that means that some operations are being prepared, which means that more personnel is mobilised in order to reinforce units and bring them up to a higher level of readiness, if that is so. But I don't think anything about that sort of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I realise I may have phrased that question wrongly. I think it was arming you were concerned about, Mr. Hannis. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you know how many of these security forces there were in Kosovo, and where they were located? Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personal knowledge, no. I was not there. I noticed them in passing. I saw a few members of that or such unit. They were present the most in Kosovska Mitrovica. There were attempts made elsewhere as well, but I don't know what their manning strength was or what the number of such units was. It is not within the domain of my personal knowledge, but it was rather what I may have overheard when discussing police matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were -- you mentioned that one of -- one of your disagreements with the OSCE was that they referred to the -- what you called the terrorists, they referred to as the KLA or the UCK. And I think you said that DZ called them terrorists once and Ciaglinski maybe a couple of times. Isn't it true that Mr. Walker also referred to them as terrorists on at least one occasion? And I direct you specifically to Exhibit 504 that Mr. Visnjic showed you today at page 50. On page 4 of that exhibit - I don't know if the witness has it there - the last sentence under paragraph number 4, which is entitled "Comment," it talks about Mr. Walker using the term "terrorist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you found it, General, the last question is translated in English as, "There are specific moments when he referred to terrorist actions as terrorists."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you present in that meeting? Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall this meeting and when he may have said this. I can't say whether Walker ever used the term terrorists. I'm sure that Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski did. I know Mr. Walker's position. He expressed on one occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General, let me --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm running out of time. I just want to ask two more questions. Mr. Cepic, on his second round today, asked you if you were aware if there was ever a plan to deport the Kosovar Albanians, and you said you were not aware of any such plan. I think at page 64, line 18 is where this first came up today -- or, I'm sorry, it's a little later. General, you were retired from the army in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that time, you never attended any VJ collegium meetings, any General Staff meetings, or any Joint Command meetings, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LONCAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I don't have any more questions for you. Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope you haven't rushed yourself unnecessarily. You obviously still have some time if you want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We were willing to give you another ten minutes beyond that if necessary, and that's why Judge Chowhan had to leave as a matter of urgency, but we were prepared to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General Loncar, that completes your evidence. Thank you for making the arrangements you did, to accommodate the Tribunal, and for coming to give evidence. That completes your involvement, and we will now terminate the videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to express the gratitude of the Trial Chamber to all who were involved in making these exceptional arrangements to ensure that the witness's evidence could be taken so far as possible over yesterday and today. We'll now adjourn for the week, and we will resume on Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: WITNESS:  It only concerned the more important incidents in Kosovo
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.52 p.m.,
